title: Eleven Beds in Madurai, Six of Them Free
dek: In 1976 a retired eye surgeon and his family mortgaged their homes to open a hospital where five paying beds had to carry six free ones.

story.founder: Govindappa Venkataswamy (Dr V), with G. Natchiar and P. Namperumalsamy
story.company: Aravind Eye Hospital, under the GOVEL Trust (now Aravind Eye Care System)
story.event: Opening an 11-bed eye hospital with six free beds after retiring at 58
story.summary: On retiring from government service at 58 in 1976, Dr G. Venkataswamy formed the GOVEL Trust with his siblings and, with no substantial donors and little access to loans, opened the 11-bed Aravind Eye Hospital in a house rented from his brother in Madurai, financed by mortgaged homes and family savings. Six beds were reserved for patients who paid nothing and five for moderately charged paying patients; the hospital ran a surplus from the start and opened a 70-bed free hospital in 1978.
paragraphs: In 1976, at 58, Govindappa Venkataswamy retired from government service as head of ophthalmology at the Government Madurai Medical College. Rheumatoid arthritis had ended his army career in 1948 and left his fingers crippled; he had trained them to hold a scalpel, and since the early 1960s he had led Tamil Nadu's mobile eye camps. Retirement did not end that work. With his brothers and sisters as trustees, he set up the GOVEL Trust to open an eye hospital of his own.

Money was the first problem. Donors the family approached would not help substantially, and loans were hard to get. Dr V was a pensioner, and the surgeons he persuaded to join him, his sister Dr G. Natchiar and her husband Dr P. Namperumalsamy, had little income. 'We weren't bankable,' Natchiar later told Forbes. The government paid towards each poor patient operated on from its eye camps, but well short of the cost. So Dr V mortgaged his house, his siblings pooled their savings, and they opened an 11-bed hospital in a house rented from his brother in Madurai.

The defining decision was how to use the eleven beds. Six were kept for patients who would pay nothing; five were for patients who would pay. Paying patients were to be charged moderately, no more than comparable hospitals in the city, rather than a few wealthy ones being made to carry the poor. Dr V was sure that only high productivity and volume could make it viable. Often asked why he took on such a task at 58, he wrote that he 'felt impelled to give something back to this great land of ours.'

It held. According to a 2003 IIM Ahmedabad teaching case written with the family's help, the hospital ran a surplus from the start. When the trust did borrow, from the State Bank of India, it pledged the trustees' own property. A 30-bed building opened in 1977, and in 1978 a 70-bed hospital for free patients only. Relatives worked long hours for very little pay. The rule outlived its founder: Aravind says about half its patients are still treated free or at steeply subsidised rates, and by 2010 its doctors were rotated between the free and paying wings.

quote.text: Finally, this is better, that one do His own task as he may, even though he fail, Than take tasks not his own, though they seem good.
quote.thinker: Bhagavad Gita (Krishna speaking; traditionally attributed to Vyasa)
quote.locator: Chapter III, 'Karma-Yog, or The Book of Virtue in Work' (verse 35 in the usual numbering)
quote.source_title: The Song Celestial; Or, Bhagavad-Gita (from the Mahabharata), translated by Sir Edwin Arnold, Project Gutenberg eBook #2388 (from the 1900 New York printing by Truslove, Hanson & Comba)
quote.connection: In 1976 nobody, Dr V included, could know whether five paying beds would carry six free ones. Arnold's Krishna makes no promise that they will. He says only that your own work, done as well as you can, is better than someone else's that looks finer.

reflection: Six free beds were a promise, and a promise like that is only as good as the care behind it. Aravind kept it by refusing to run two standards: the same doctors, whatever the patient paid. That is a quality decision as much as a moral one, and it sits close to why talQen exists. A result for a patient who cannot pay should be as trustworthy as any other, and what makes that true is mostly unglamorous: checks, records and routines kept on ordinary days.
You do not need all of talQen working to be doing your own task well. Eleven beds were enough to begin.
invitation: Ask one lab colleague today which quality check is the first to slip on a busy day. Write the answer down for talQen, then leave it there until tomorrow.

cross_checks.claim: Dr V retired from government service in 1976 at the age of 58.
Aravind opened in Madurai in 1976 with 11 beds.
Six of the eleven beds were reserved for patients who paid nothing; five were for paying patients.
The hospital was financed by mortgaged homes and family savings rather than donors.
The first hospital was in a house belonging to, and rented from, Dr V's brother.
About half of Aravind's patients are treated free or at subsidised rates, paid for by the other half.

research_notes: Premises: Forbes says the clinic was in a house rented from Dr V's brother and the IIM Ahmedabad case says it was in his brother's house; Conversations.org and Caravan say a rented house; India Together places it in a rented house at Theni, which conflicts with every other source and was not used. Aravind's own page says Dr V mortgaged his house to fund the hospital, which concerns financing, not premises. Bed count: Aravind, the IIM case, Forbes, Scroll and the Indian Journal of Ophthalmology all give 11; a few secondary pages say 10 or 20. The six-free/five-paying split comes from the IIM case and Scroll (a Quartz piece drawing on a Bridgespan case study); The News Minute's 2018 Google Doodle article agrees. Loans: Forbes says loans were hard to get, while the IIM case says the trust did borrow from the State Bank of India by pledging trustees' property in the early years; the story reports both. The 1977 (30-bed) and 1978 (70-bed free) expansions rest on the IIM case alone (teaching slides elsewhere give 100 beds for 1978), so the prose attributes them to the case. Forbes's $55,000 seed-capital figure is single-sourced and was left out. Later figures conflict (the IIM case gives a 250-bed paying hospital in 1981; a Conversations.org timeline gives a 600-bed hospital), so the story stops at 1978. The rotation of doctors between wings is reported by Forbes in 2010; the prose dates it accordingly. Dr V's words 'felt impelled to give something back to this great land of ours' are quoted in the IIM case from Aravind's 2001 publication Promises to Keep, which was not fetched directly. The IIM case link is an Internet Archive copy of a PDF formerly on Brown University's wiki; it loads (HTTP 200). Quote: Arnold's translation was first published in 1885; the Gutenberg text is the 1900 New York printing, whose front matter names Arnold as translator. Arnold does not number verses; the passage is the end of Chapter III, verse 35 in standard numbering. Sri Aurobindo is not quoted.
